text: Standard gravity is defined as 9.80665 metres per second squared.
source: BIPM SI Brochure; 3rd General Conference on Weights and Measures, 1901

text: Earth's mass is about 5.97 x 10^24 kg, roughly six trillion trillion kilograms.
source: NASA Goddard Earth Fact Sheet

text: Doubling surface gravity gives roughly 19.6 metres per second squared.
source: Derived: 2 x 9.80665 m/s^2 (BIPM standard gravity)

text: A 70 kg person has a weight of about 686 newtons, which is about 690.
source: Derived from F = mg with BIPM standard gravity

text: At doubled gravity the same person's weight is about 1,373 newtons.
source: Derived from F = mg with doubled standard gravity

text: Fall time from 1 m at standard gravity is about 0.45 seconds.
source: Derived from t = sqrt(2h/g), with BIPM standard gravity

text: Fall time from 1 m at doubled gravity is about 0.32 seconds.
source: Derived from t = sqrt(2h/g) with g doubled

text: Impact speed rises by a factor of the square root of two, about 1.4.
source: Derived from v = sqrt(2gh)

text: A half-metre jump becomes a quarter-metre jump at the same take-off speed.
source: Derived from h = v^2/2g

text: Fighter pilots with training and suits can sustain about nine g.
source: US Air Force and NASA centrifuge and aircraft g-tolerance literature; F-16 9 g design limit

text: Untrained people typically lose vision or consciousness at around four to six g.
source: NASA and US Air Force aerospace physiology references on g-induced loss of consciousness

text: A fall from 3 m at doubled gravity has the energy of a fall from 6 m at normal gravity.
as_written: A fall from three metres tonight hits like a fall from six metres yesterday
source: Derived from E = mgh

text: A 1.7 m person's head would hit the floor at about 8.2 m/s at doubled gravity versus 5.8 m/s normally.
as_written: about 8.2 metres per second instead of 5.8
source: Derived from v = sqrt(2gh) with h = 1.7 m

text: More than one in four adults aged 65 and older falls each year.
as_written: more than one in four adults aged sixty-five and older falls every year
source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, STEADI older adult fall prevention

text: The tallest known tree, the coast redwood Hyperion, is about 116 metres.
source: US National Park Service, Redwood National and State Parks; Earle, Gymnosperm Database

text: Koch et al. estimated the maximum height of redwoods at about 122 to 130 metres.
source: Koch, Sillett, Jennings and Davis, The limits to tree height, Nature, 2004

text: Standard sea-level atmospheric pressure is 101,325 pascals.
source: ISO 2533 / ICAO International Standard Atmosphere

text: Ten metres of seawater adds about one atmosphere of pressure, so doubling surface pressure matches about ten metres depth.
as_written: about ten metres below the surface of the sea
source: NOAA Diving Manual; US Navy Diving Manual

text: The speed of sound near the surface is about 340 m/s.
source: ISO 2533 standard atmosphere (340.3 m/s at sea level, 15 C)

text: Earth's atmospheric scale height is about 8.5 km, and halves if gravity doubles.
as_written: from about 8.5 kilometres to about four
source: NASA Goddard Earth Fact Sheet (scale height 8.5 km); halving derived from H = kT/mg

text: Oxygen is about 21 percent of air by volume.
source: NOAA / NASA atmospheric composition data (20.95 percent)

text: At two atmospheres of air the oxygen partial pressure is about 0.42 atmospheres.
source: Derived: 0.21 x 2 atm

text: Divers keep oxygen partial pressure below 1.4 atmospheres during working dives.
source: NOAA Diving Manual; US Navy Diving Manual oxygen exposure limits

text: The ISS orbits about 400 km up at about 7.66 km/s, with a period of about 92 minutes.
as_written: about 400 kilometres above the ground, at about 7.66 kilometres per second, and completes an orbit in about 92 minutes
source: NASA International Space Station facts

text: Circular orbital speed at doubled mass is about 10.8 km/s.
source: Derived: 7.66 km/s x sqrt(2), vis-viva equation

text: After the change, the perigee of a formerly circular orbit lies at one third of its radius.
as_written: one third of the station's current distance
source: Derived from the vis-viva equation with doubled mu

text: The ISS is about 6,770 km from Earth's centre; a third is about 2,300 km.
source: Derived from NASA ISS altitude and Earth mean radius

text: Earth's mean radius is about 6,371 km.
source: NASA Goddard Earth Fact Sheet

text: The station reaches the bottom of its new orbit in under twenty minutes, half of a roughly 36-minute new period.
source: Derived from Kepler's third law with doubled mu and semi-major axis two thirds of r

text: There are more than ten thousand active satellites in orbit.
as_written: more than ten thousand working satellites
source: Union of Concerned Scientists Satellite Database; Jonathan McDowell, Jonathan's Space Report

text: Geostationary orbit is about 35,786 km above the equator.
source: ESA and NASA geostationary orbit reference values

text: The Moon's mean distance is about 384,400 km and its orbital speed is about 1.02 km/s.
as_written: about 384,400 kilometres, moving at a little over one kilometre per second
source: NASA Goddard Moon Fact Sheet

text: The Moon's new perigee would be one third of the current distance, about 128,000 km.
source: Derived from the vis-viva equation: 384,400 / 3

text: The Moon's sidereal period is 27.3 days, falling to about 10.5 days.
as_written: from 27.3 days to about ten and a half days
source: NASA Goddard Moon Fact Sheet (27.3 days); new value derived from Kepler's third law with a = 2r/3 and doubled mu

text: Tidal force scales as the inverse cube of distance, so one third the distance gives 27 times the force.
source: Newtonian tidal theory; derived 3 cubed = 27

text: The Sun is about 333,000 times Earth's mass.
as_written: about 333,000 times more massive than the Earth
source: NASA Goddard Sun Fact Sheet

text: The year is about 365.25 days.
source: IAU / Julian year definition, 365.25 days

text: The average ocean depth is about 3,700 metres.
source: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, ETOPO global relief (mean depth about 3,688 m)

text: Long-wave speed is sqrt(g x depth): about 690 km/h at normal gravity and about 970 km/h at doubled gravity for 3,700 m depth.
source: NOAA Tsunami Program shallow-water wave speed formula; values derived

text: Doubled gravity gives roughly 970 km/h for the same depth.
source: Derived from sqrt(2 x 9.80665 x 3,700 m)

text: Earth's escape velocity is 11.2 km/s, rising by root two to about 15.8 km/s.
as_written: from 11.2 to about 15.8 kilometres per second
source: NASA Goddard Earth Fact Sheet (11.186 km/s); new value derived

text: Astronauts lose roughly 1 to 1.5 percent of bone mineral density per month in the hips and spine in orbit.
as_written: one to one and a half percent per month
source: NASA Human Research Program, bone loss in spaceflight

text: Ingenuity flew in Martian air about one percent as dense as Earth's, in 2021.
as_written: about one percent as dense as ours
source: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Mars Helicopter Ingenuity mission

text: Required level-flight power rises roughly in proportion to weight to the 1.5 over the square root of density, giving about double at doubled weight and density.
source: Derived from actuator-disc and induced-power theory, e.g. Pennycuick, Modelling the Flying Bird
